newsitem.title: INDIA: Bombay Hindus bid goodbye to elephant god Ganesha.
newsitem.headline: Bombay Hindus bid goodbye to elephant god Ganesha.

text.p: Hundreds of thousands of Hindu devotees bid a noisy farewell to the elephant god Ganesha on Thursday by immersing his idols in the sea.
Beating drums and dancing along the crowded roads of India's commercial capital Bombay, devotees made their way to scores of beaches for the climax of a 10-day festival.
The immersions celebrate the birth of Ganesha, the son of Lord Shiva, the Hindu god of destruction and his consort Parvati.
"Ganapati bappa moriya (long live Lord Ganesha)", chanted the devotees amid ear- shattering blasts from fire-crackers.
Ganesha came in all shapes and sizes, from tiny idols carried on the heads of devotees to giants weighing a few tonnes that required trucks to haul them.
There was Ganesha dancing on the hood of a snake, another sitting on a lotus and another as a manifestation of Lord Vishnu, the allusions drawn from Hindu mythological lore.
Saffron flags atop the trucks carrying the idols fluttered in the evening sea breeze, spreading a mild fragrance from the marigold flowers showered by devotees.
At the main immersion site, Chowpatty Beach in south Bombay, police set up scores of lifeguard towers.
"It's all quiet," said a fire brigade official. "We are only worried that some devotees might come drunk and wander into the sea," the official said.
Two speed boats cruised along at a distance as the devotees waded into the sea with the idols. Helicopters hovered overhead.
The state of Maharashtra, of which Bombay is the capital, declared a holiday and most private businesses closed early to help them avoid traffic jams during the processions.
The authorities banned the sale of liquor and ordered the closure of all bars across the state for the day.
Chowpatty Beach resembled a carnival with shops, food stalls, and children's rides.
As darkness descended on the city, the floodlights at Chowpatty gave the atmosphere a mythological aura.
"Pudcha varshi lowkar ya (come early next year)," the devotees chanted as they bid their god a fond farewell.
